title_original: Thomas Savary: At the Salers’ Pace
excerpt_original: Every year at the end of May, the small town of Allanche, in the Cantal region in France, escorts its Salers herds up to the high pastures. Thomas Savary photographed the Fête de l'Estive there with a Sigma fp, following the gestures that pass from one generation to the next.…

blocks.text: Here, the cow is set in stone. On the Place du Cézallier, a cow and her calf carved from lava have watched over Allanche since 1996, placid sentinels of a town of some 770 souls perched at 1,100 meters (plenty of fresh air to go around). The rest of the year, the little basalt town moves at the slow pace of the plateau. At the end of May, everything tips over. Bells, hooves, brass bands, the smell of aligot and fritters: nearly 40,000 visitors come up to greet the herds bound for the summer pastures, and the village dreams of being a capital. Capital of what? Of transhumance, of truffade, of time that passes without passing. Thomas Savary went up quietly, to follow what is handed down from one hand to the next. A matter of horns and heart.

Photographer Thomas Savary did not come alone. In May 2025, Vincent Pietri, a longtime friend based in Aurillac, proposed, together with Allanche’s town hall, to tell the story of the festival through four different eyes. With Jérémy Laurichesse and Roméo Ichard, they covered both days of the Estive. “Between truffade and aligot, we roamed the event, photographing the herds as well as local crafts, the breeders, the residents and the public,” he recalls. The images found a first audience at the Regards en Cézallier festival, then during a five-day residency at Artopia, the cultural venue Vincent Pietri developed in Aurillac. A traveling exhibition came out of it. It circulated among local partners, from a car dealership to the departmental council.

Thomas set his rule from the start: no stolen pictures. “I never hid the fact that I was taking pictures,” he says. The camera, a Sigma fp chosen for its discreet size, served first of all to start conversations, to ask questions, to understand who does what. “Photography then became less an end in itself than a pretext for creating a connection,” he continues. He showed the screen to the people he had just photographed, and sometimes took down their contact details to send them the images later. The support of the town hall, and especially of mayor Philippe Rosseel, opened the breeders’ doors to him.

Thomas Savary often tightens the frame down to the detail, in a series made up exclusively of vertical images: two hands crossed on a shepherd’s staff, a scarf held by a small wooden clog. The device is familiar, and it has its limits. With so many fragments, the series at times verges on rustic imagery, a catalog of accessories. Yet here it serves a precise purpose. By leaving out faces, the photographer shifts the portrait toward the tool and the garment, in other words toward what is passed on. It is in these tight images that his statement on heritage finds its clearest form.

And then there is the child. Straight bangs, a hoodie printed with cartoon puppies, he brushes an animal’s flank with a sure hand and stares into the lens, brow furrowed, as if interrupted at work. Behind him, out of focus, an adult stands with arms crossed. “I’m thinking in particular of the photograph of this child with his brush, reproducing a gesture that his great-grandfather probably made before him,” Thomas Savary explains. The gesture is old; the hoodie is new. “It’s precisely this contrast that interests me,” he adds. On one side, gestures that cross the generations unchanged; on the other, thoroughly contemporary habits. The Estive, as the artist puts it, becomes the place where these two timeframes coexist.

The animals, then, get their own portraits. A cow faces the camera head-on, horns spread like handlebars, two yellow tags on her ears marked 6659. A thread of drool hangs from her muzzle. Neither endearing nor threatening, she is simply a presence. Thomas Savary remembers a breeder showing him a bull that had won a prize at the Paris Salon de l’Agriculture, and “the love and pride with which he spoke about his work, his skills and his animals.” Facing an animal that can weigh more than a ton, he describes “a mix of excitement, admiration and, I must admit, a little fear.”

On Sunday morning, the festival sets off. The breeders drive their herds from Allanche to Pradiers, a four- to five-hour walk, and the crowd follows. In an image taken from a distance, under a heavy sky, the procession is nothing more than a line of colors, anoraks and backpacks, running along the road at the foot of a hill, between the power poles. “There is something almost timeless about this ascent, at once deeply traditional and incredibly alive,” says the photographer. Higher up, a dry-stone buron (a shepherd’s hut) roofed with sheet metal hunkers down in the grass, yellow flowers in the foreground. And finally, on the ridge, a herd grazes in single file, barely bigger than grains of rice. That too is the Estive: what remains once the festival has passed.

Honestly, the series changed shape quite a bit with Sigma. The Japanese company has been producing very high-end equipment for some years, and Thomas Savary shared his images with the brand whose camera he uses. Sigma, present in Arles this year for the sixth consecutive year, offered him a show in the Off program during the opening week of the Rencontres de la photographie 2026. Shortly before, from January to June, he reworked the edit with Sigma’s teams and independent curator Audrey Hoareau, thought through the scenography, and prepared a book. The title tightened: “L’Estive” (The Summer Pasture). From July 6 to 12, on Rue du Pont, the prints were pasted on the wall and accompanied by a soundtrack of three minutes and thirty-six seconds by the photographer.

On October 11, Thomas Savary looks back on the whole project at the Salon Photo & Vidéo, the new name of the Salon de la Photo, at the Grande Halle de la Villette in Paris. In Sigma’s Rencontres space, he retraces the path from shooting with the fp to the hanging in Arles. In Allanche as in Arles, he says, the response was warm. The 35th Fête de l’Estive is scheduled for May 22 and 23, 2027, in Allanche.

Thomas Savary presents “L’Estive” on Sunday October 11, 2026, in Sigma’s Rencontres space at the Salon Photo & Vidéo, held October 8 to 11, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., at the Grande Halle de la Villette in Paris. Sigma is offering free tickets with the code SIGMA26 on sigma-photo.fr . More of the photographer’s work is on his website .
